What is Biodiversity?

Biodiversity (biological diversity) is the variety of all life on Earth – plants, animals, fungi and microbes – together with the ecosystems they form and the genetic differences inside each species. The term was popularised in the 1980s, and it is often described at three levels:

DNAGenetic
varieties within a species
SPPSpecies
variety of different species
ECOEcosystem
variety of habitats

Major Ecosystems

Forests

Home to over half of land species; they store carbon and make rain.

Oceans & Coral Reefs

Reefs cover under 1% of the seabed yet shelter around a quarter of marine species.

Deserts

Specially adapted plants and animals survive extreme heat and little water.

Mangroves & Wetlands

Nurseries for fish, natural storm barriers – like the Sundarbans of West Bengal.

Ecosystem Services – What Nature Gives Us

Scientists group the benefits of biodiversity into four types of "ecosystem services". Losing species weakens every one of them.

Provisioning

  • Food: crops, fish, fruits, honey
  • Fresh water and timber
  • Medicines – many drugs come from plants, fungi and microbes
  • Fibres such as cotton, jute and silk

Regulating

  • Forests and oceans absorb carbon dioxide
  • Wetlands and mangroves filter water and cut flood and storm damage
  • Bees, birds and bats pollinate – about three-quarters of leading food crops benefit from animal pollination
  • Predators control pests

Supporting

  • Soil formation and nutrient cycling by earthworms, fungi and bacteria
  • Photosynthesis and the oxygen we breathe
  • Habitat for every other species

Cultural

  • Sacred groves, rivers and animals in Indian traditions
  • Tourism, recreation and mental well-being
  • Inspiration for art, music and science
The food web: every organism is linked. Producers (plants, algae) are eaten by herbivores, which are eaten by carnivores, while decomposers return nutrients to the soil. Remove a keystone species, such as a top predator or a key pollinator, and the effects ripple through the whole web.

Biodiversity in India

India is one of 17 megadiverse countries, holding roughly 7–8% of the world's recorded species on only about 2.4% of its land area. It contains four global biodiversity hotspots:

HIMHimalaya
WGWestern Ghats
IBIndo-Burma
NICNicobar Islands (Sundaland)

Close to home: the Sundarbans in West Bengal is the world's largest mangrove forest and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, famous for the Royal Bengal Tiger, saltwater crocodiles and hundreds of bird species.

Timeline: Protecting Life

1971 – Ramsar Convention

First global treaty to protect wetlands.

1972 – Wildlife (Protection) Act, India

Legal protection for wild animals, plants and habitats; created national parks and sanctuaries.

1973 – Project Tiger

Launched in India to save the tiger through dedicated reserves.

1992 – Rio Earth Summit

The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was opened for signature; it came into force in 1993.

2002 – Biological Diversity Act, India

Regulates access to biological resources and shares benefits with local communities.

2022 – Kunming-Montreal Framework

Global agreement with the "30 by 30" goal: protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.

Main Threats

Ordered by overall impact, as ranked by the IPBES Global Assessment (2019).

1. Land & sea use change (habitat loss)
2. Direct exploitation (overfishing, poaching)
3. Climate change
4. Pollution (plastic, chemicals)
5. Invasive alien species

How Do We Conserve Biodiversity?

In-situ (on site)

Protecting species in their natural home.

  • National parks and wildlife sanctuaries
  • Biosphere reserves (e.g. Sundarbans)
  • Sacred groves protected by communities
  • Community and conservation reserves

Ex-situ (off site)

Protecting species outside their habitat.

  • Zoos and breeding programmes
  • Botanical gardens
  • Seed banks and gene banks
  • Cryopreservation of cells
Success story: Project Tiger and strict protection helped India become home to the majority of the world's wild tigers, showing that recovery is possible when people, policy and habitat work together.

Why It Matters & What We Can Do

Biodiversity gives us food, medicines, clean water, pollination and a stable climate. Protecting it is protecting ourselves.

Plant

Plant native trees and keep green spaces alive.

Reduce

Cut single-use plastic; reuse and recycle.

Save

Conserve water and energy every day.

Spread

Tell friends and family. Never buy wildlife products.

Did You Know?

  • One bee colony can visit millions of flowers in a season – without pollinators, many of our fruits would vanish.
  • Fungi networks under forest soil help trees share nutrients.
  • Coral reefs cover a tiny fraction of the ocean floor but support enormous marine life.
  • Scientists estimate most species on Earth are still undescribed – especially insects and deep-sea life.
  • India once grew tens of thousands of rice varieties; preserving them protects future food security.
